stated.value: In-line NIR pilot measuring API concentration at the tablet press feed frame
Introducing a different API and a different excipient blend
Reuse the existing NIR calibration for the new blend
Add Raman so that the old calibration remains valid
First technical assessment and first experiment

missing: Identity of the new API and its concentration range
Excipient composition of the new blend and what changed versus the old one
Existing NIR calibration details: wavelength range, spectral pre-processing, PLS/model type, number of factors, calibration range and RMSEP
Reference method used for calibration (e.g. HPLC) and its precision
Probe type, optical path and window material at the feed frame, and the current install geometry
Acceptance criteria for the new method (e.g. allowed bias or prediction error in % of target)
Whether the new blend's excipients or API are fluorescent, strongly colored or highly absorbing in the NIR or Raman range
Powder properties of the new blend (particle size, density, flow, moisture) and feed frame throughput
Regulatory or quality context (e.g. PAT use for release versus process monitoring)

status_reason: The core question can be answered from general spectroscopy principles, but the specific chemistry, calibration details and acceptance criteria are not yet known, so the answer stays provisional.
answer: Adding Raman will not by itself keep the old NIR calibration valid: a regression model is specific to the spectral method, the spectral features and the matrix it was built on, and a change in API and excipients alters both. The first step is a calibration-transfer test: measure the existing NIR model on samples of the new blend against a reference method, and check bias, slope and error to decide whether the calibration transfers, needs updating, or needs a new model. Raman can be tested in parallel as a complementary method, but only as a separate calibration built on the new blend.

inline.headline: Keep the in-line NIR at the feed frame as the production-oriented method, test calibration transfer first, and evaluate Raman as a separate, complementary method rather than as a way to preserve the NIR calibration.
inline.method: Primary: NIR (existing) with a calibration-transfer assessment on the new blend. Secondary: Raman evaluated for its own calibration on the new blend, and optionally as a combined NIR+Raman model if both are feasible in-line.
inline.probe: Retain the existing NIR probe geometry at the feed frame for the baseline. For Raman, use a non-contact or immersion-free fiber probe with a suitable working distance focused on the powder surface at the feed frame, with a window that does not foul from powder dust. Check the probe for fluorescence background from the excipients.
inline.install: Mount the Raman probe next to or at the same measurement point as the NIR probe so both see the same powder stream. Protect the optics from dust and vibration, and confirm the spot is representative of the blend in the feed frame.
inline.fiber: Use low-OH silica fiber for NIR and suitable Raman fiber with low background fluorescence. Keep fiber lengths short to limit losses and interference from the press environment.
inline.test_against: Reference values from a validated lab method (e.g. HPLC) on samples of the new blend across the planned concentration range, plus offline samples from the feed frame at multiple time points. Compare NIR predictions of the old calibration with the reference values.
inline.not_final_because: The API identity, the calibration details, the excipient effects, the reference-method precision and the acceptance criteria are unknown. The spectroscopic behaviour of the new blend has not been measured, so the transfer outcome and the value of Raman cannot be judged yet.

problems.text: Adding Raman does not preserve the NIR calibration. A regression model maps one method's spectra to concentration; a different technique produces different spectra and therefore needs its own calibration. Raman cannot make the old NIR model valid.

The old calibration is assumed to remain valid after the API and excipient change. Changes in API, excipients, particle size or density alter the spectral baseline, band overlaps and scattering, so predictions can shift even when the target concentration is the same.
Whether the existing NIR model transfers to the new blend is unknown. This must be tested on the new blend against a reference method before any decision on recalibration.

The new API or excipients may fluoresce under Raman excitation, or may absorb strongly in the NIR range, which could swamp the signal of interest. Check the spectra of the pure components before committing to Raman.
Feed frame sampling may be non-representative because of powder segregation or uneven flow. Both methods measure only a small spot, so the sampling point and sample volume need to be assessed.

methods.why: It is already installed and validated for the old blend, so it is the baseline and the first candidate for calibration transfer. Its suitability for the new blend has to be proven, not assumed.

Raman gives sharp, specific bands that are often less affected by water and by the broad overlaps seen in NIR, so it may be more robust to some changes in formulation. It needs its own calibration and must be checked for fluorescence from excipients.

Worth considering only if each method alone is inadequate and the combined data improve prediction. It adds cost, complexity and a second calibration effort, so it should follow the single-method results.

methods.method: Calibration transfer or model update of existing NIR (e.g. slope/bias correction or augmented calibration)
methods.why: This is the direct route to reusing the NIR investment. It may work if the new blend is close to the old one, but it must be validated with a bias test and, if needed, extra calibration samples from the new blend.
Neither is a typical in-line feed frame method for this application and neither is needed for the enquiry. They would add risk and cost without a clear advantage over NIR or Raman.

questions.q: What are the API and the excipients in the new blend, and what is the target concentration range?
questions.why: Specific absorbers, fluorescent components or overlapping bands determine which method is viable and how difficult the transfer will be.

questions.q: What are the details of the existing NIR calibration: spectral range, pre-processing, model type, factors, calibration range and RMSEP?
questions.why: These determine whether the model can be transferred, corrected or must be rebuilt, and what performance the new blend must match.

questions.q: Which reference method was used for the old calibration, and what is its precision?
questions.why: The achievable accuracy of any new calibration cannot exceed the precision of the reference data.

questions.q: What acceptance criteria apply to the in-line method (e.g. maximum bias or prediction error as a percentage of target)?
questions.why: These define the go/no-go decision and the required number of calibration and validation samples.

questions.q: Is the new blend's particle size, density or flow significantly different from the old blend?
questions.why: Physical changes affect scattering and sampling, which can shift the spectra independently of concentration.

questions.q: Is the measurement intended for process monitoring only or for release decisions?
questions.why: This determines the level of validation, documentation and regulatory scrutiny required.

questions.q: Is there room at the feed frame for a second probe, and is the existing NIR probe window and geometry known?
questions.why: The installation constraints decide whether NIR and Raman can measure the same powder stream.

experiment.objective: Determine whether the existing NIR calibration transfers to the new API and excipient blend, and whether Raman offers a viable independent or complementary calibration, using reference-verified samples before any in-line change is made.
steps: Obtain the existing NIR calibration documentation and the old-blend spectra and reference values.

Confirm the new blend's composition and prepare a calibration set of the new blend across the target concentration range, covering the expected variation of excipients and physical properties, with reference values from the validated lab method.
Record NIR spectra of the new blend samples with the existing pilot setup at the feed frame or with a laboratory equivalent using the same optics and geometry.
Predict the new blend samples with the old NIR calibration and compare predictions with the reference values. Calculate bias, slope, intercept, RMSEP and R-squared, and check for outliers.

If bias or slope is outside acceptance criteria, apply a simple transfer correction (slope/bias) and retest on an independent validation set, or build an augmented or new NIR model from the new blend data.
In parallel, record Raman spectra of the pure API, the pure excipients and the new blend to check for fluorescence and band specificity.
If the Raman spectra are usable, build a Raman calibration on the new blend with the same reference values and validate on an independent set.
Compare the NIR-transferred, NIR-updated and Raman models on the same validation samples and select the best, or test a combined model only if neither is adequate.
Only after lab success, carry out an in-line trial at the feed frame with reference samples taken during the press run to confirm performance under real process conditions.
references: Calibration transfer in NIR spectroscopy (e.g. Workman and Shenk; Feudale et al., Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems, on calibration transfer methods)
ICH Q2(R2) on validation of analytical procedures
FDA Process Analytical Technology (PAT) framework guidance (2004) and ICH Q14 on analytical procedure development
Pharmaceutical NIR and Raman applications literature, e.g. Clarke et al. and Ruiz-Montoya et al. on API quantification in tablet blends
experiment.go_no_go: Go for NIR transfer if the bias and slope on an independent validation set of the new blend fall within the agreed acceptance criteria (e.g. bias and RMSEP within the allowed percentage of target) and the spectra show no unacceptable interference. Go for Raman only if its spectra are free of excessive fluorescence and its validated model meets the same criteria. No-go for in-line deployment with the old calibration if neither method meets the criteria without a new calibration effort, in which case plan a full recalibration with new-blend samples.

multispectral.combination: Test NIR and Raman on the same samples and compare single-method models first; evaluate a fused or data-level combined model only if one or both single models fail the acceptance criteria.
multispectral.why: The two techniques probe different vibrational modes and can be complementary, which may reduce the effect of excipient or physical changes. However, a combined model is not a way to retain the old calibration and it increases complexity, so it should be justified by the single-method results.

assumptions: The new blend is measured with the same pilot physical setup and sampling point as the old blend, unless otherwise stated.
The reference method for concentration is validated and precise enough to support calibration and transfer decisions.
The target concentration range of the new API is comparable to the old one, and the API is present at a level detectable by NIR and/or Raman.
The existing NIR pilot hardware and software are functional and can be used for the lab or in-line tests.
Raman is considered only as a separate or complementary method, and not as a means to make the old NIR calibration valid.
Regulatory expectations are those of process monitoring or PAT unless the enquirer states that release decisions are intended.
